title: Managed Identity with Key Vault
description: Connect an Azure-managed identity to Key Vault so your app can read secrets without storing any credentials.

data.text: When your app has a managed identity, it can request an access token from Entra ID. You then grant that identity access to Key Vault. Your app uses the token to call Key Vault APIs — no connection string or secret required.

data.title: Steps to Connect Managed Identity to Key Vault
items: Enable a system-assigned managed identity on your app.
Create a Key Vault access policy or RBAC role assignment for the identity.
Grant the identity Get permission on secrets.
Use DefaultAzureCredential in code to authenticate.

data.title: Assign Key Vault Access Policy with Azure CLI
data.content: Give a managed identity permission to read secrets from a Key Vault.
data.code: az keyvault set-policy   --name myKeyVault   --object-id "managed-identity-principal-id"   --secret-permissions get list

data.title: Read a Secret with Managed Identity (C#)
data.content: Use DefaultAzureCredential — in Azure it picks up the managed identity automatically.

data.title: Connect an App to Key Vault
data.description: Enable a managed identity on an App Service, create a Key Vault secret, and assign the app access to read it.
steps: Create an App Service and enable its system-assigned managed identity.
Create a Key Vault and add a secret named 'DemoSecret' with value 'hello-world'.
Use Azure CLI to set a Key Vault access policy for the app's identity.
Write a simple API endpoint that returns the secret value.
data.expectedOutcome: Your API returns the secret from Key Vault without any connection string or password in code.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Managed identity + Key Vault means zero secrets in code.
DefaultAzureCredential works everywhere — local dev with Azure CLI, CI with service principal, and Azure with managed identity.
Always scope Key Vault permissions to the minimum needed (e.g., get and list only).
